questions.prompt: How does the compiler handle a #include "config.hpp" directive before phase 7 semantic analysis begins?
options: It compiles config.hpp once into a cached symbol table shared across all .cpp files.
It defers resolving declarations in config.hpp until the linker merges object files in phase 9.
The preprocessor textually pastes config.hpp into the including file in phase 4 to form one translation unit.
It automatically assigns internal linkage to every function declared inside config.hpp.
questions.explanation: Under [lex.phases], preprocessing in phase 4 textually inserts the contents of included headers and expands macros. Phase 7 parses the resulting single translation unit with no separate concept of a header file.

questions.prompt: You need a helper struct Buffer defined in two different .cpp files with different layouts and no ODR collision. Which declaration gives Buffer internal linkage?
options: namespace { struct Buffer { int len; }; }
static struct Buffer { int len; };
inline struct Buffer { int len; };
extern "C" struct Buffer { int len; };
questions.explanation: An unnamed namespace gives internal linkage to every declaration inside it, including class types and templates. The static specifier cannot be applied to a class definition itself.

questions.prompt: Why does putting this header snippet into two translation units violate the One Definition Rule?
options: A const variable cannot have its address taken at namespace scope.
Returning a pointer from an inline function makes it non-inline.
Taking &kRetries forces dynamic initialization across translation units.
kRetries has internal linkage by default, so retry_ptr() resolves to a different object in each TU (IFNDR).
questions.explanation: A namespace-scope const variable without extern or inline has internal linkage under [basic.link], giving each TU its own kRetries object. Because retry_ptr() has external linkage and its odr-used name kRetries resolves to different entities across TUs, the program violates [basic.def.odr] (IFNDR). Adding inline constexpr fixes this.

questions.prompt: What happens if a header included by two .cpp files contains `extern "C" { int shared_status; }`?
options: It compiles and links cleanly because extern suppresses allocating storage.
Linking fails with a duplicate definition error because braces restrict extern "C" to language linkage only.
shared_status automatically receives internal linkage in each translation unit.
It is ill-formed at compile time because variables cannot have C language linkage.
questions.explanation: Inside a braced linkage-specification (`extern "C" { ... }`), extern specifies language linkage rather than external-declaration-only status ([dcl.link]). Therefore `int shared_status;` is a variable definition in every TU that includes the header.

questions.prompt: What are the scope, storage duration, and linkage of `hits` in this inline function?
options: Block scope, static storage duration, and no linkage (yet shared across TUs via bump's ODR identity).
Block scope, automatic storage duration, and external linkage.
Namespace scope, static storage duration, and internal linkage.
Block scope, static storage duration, and external linkage.
questions.explanation: A block-scope static variable has block scope, static storage duration, and no linkage ([basic.link]). However, [dcl.inline] requires that static local variables inside an inline function with external linkage refer to the same single object across all translation units.

questions.prompt: Under [basic.link], which namespace-scope declaration still has external linkage in C++17 and later?
options: const int port = 8080;
constexpr int port = 8080;
inline constexpr int port = 8080;
namespace { constexpr int port = 8080; }
questions.explanation: Both `const` and `constexpr` at namespace scope imply const and yield internal linkage by default unless declared `inline` or `extern` (outside an unnamed namespace). Marking a constexpr variable `inline` gives it external linkage and merges all TU definitions into one object.
